clue.text: Building dams after obtaining property in the country

indicators.note: building means constructing something new, so these letters are put together afresh in another order

explanation.surface: A farmer acquires rural land and puts up dams afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Building' looks like the definition, but it is the anagram signal; 'obtaining' only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A farmstead is a farm with its buildings, a holding of land out in rural parts.

clue.text: Suddenly knock without real reason

parts.note: a knock on a door is a rap
doing something idly is doing it with no purpose or real reason

explanation.surface: Someone raps at the door all at once, for no good reason.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something happening very fast, with no time passing first.

clue.text: The band (quartet) will in-elude new item, but the music's repetitive

indicators.note: a playful spelling of 'include', saying the band's word takes something inside it

parts.note: a band of people is a lot, a group

indicators.note: new tells us the letters of item are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: a quartet is four, IV in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A band's four players work a new number into their set, though the tune keeps repeating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will in-elude' is a pun on 'include'. The definition is loose: a leitmotiv is the music's repetitive theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A leitmotiv is a recurring musical theme tied to a character or idea, as in Wagner's operas.

clue.text: Not favouring procedure, arrange a meeting

parts.note: con means against, as in the pros and cons
a course of action is a procedure

explanation.surface: An organiser, disliking the usual process, sets up a get-together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrange' has no job in the wordplay as printed; the definition is the final words.
explanation.definitionFit: A concourse is a gathering of people, a crowd that has come together.

clue.text: Appear submissive or have a ding-dong in the Church?

indicators.note: in tells us one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
a bell goes ding-dong when it rings

explanation.surface: Asks whether to be meek or to quarrel inside the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ding-dong' looks like British slang for a row, but here it is the sound of a bell ringing.
explanation.definitionFit: To cringe is to cower or shrink back in a servile, fawning way.

clue.text: Good stuff, cold remains with water!

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold on a tap
ash is what remains after burning
a mere is a lake, a stretch of water

explanation.surface: Praise for something left out in the cold, now sodden with water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stuff' means fabric here, and 'Good' says it is of fine quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is a fine, soft wool cloth, so a high-quality material.

clue.text: Downs, oddly enough

parts.note: the downs are rolling hills, so despite their name they are high ground, which is the odd part

explanation.definitionFit: The Downs are chalk hills in southern England, high ground despite their name.

clue.text: A woman with articles to put into a case

parts.note: she is the pronoun for a woman
a is the indefinite article
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A woman with some goods to pack away in a suitcase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'articles' gives both of English's articles, A and THE, in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: To sheathe a sword or knife is to slide it into its scabbard.

clue.text: A properly mature layman

indicators.note: properly suggests the letters of mature are put into proper order

explanation.surface: A grown-up person with no professional training.
explanation.walkthrough: 'properly' is the anagram signal, rearranging MATURE behind the A.
explanation.definitionFit: An amateur is a non-professional, a lay person in the field.

clue.text: Added note to change a book

parts.note: PS, postscript, is a note added to a letter
to alter is to change

explanation.surface: An instruction to tack a note on so a volume reads differently.
explanation.definitionFit: A psalter is a volume of the Psalms, used in church services.

clue.text: The doctor is very young — and so wet!

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, an army doctor
ten years old is very young

explanation.surface: A doctor is surprised that a mere child is so damp.
explanation.definitionFit: To moisten something is to dampen it, make it slightly damp.

clue.text: Begin a new life

parts.note: reads like someone starting over, but describes a seed starting to grow

explanation.definitionFit: A seed that germinates sprouts, beginning to grow into a plant.

clue.text: Her Majesty entrances the little worker

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen
gates are entrances

explanation.surface: The Queen's gateways let through a small servant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entrances' looks like a verb meaning charms, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergates are worker ants, small sterile females that labour for the colony.

clue.text: Reason for thanks-weekend in lover's embrace

parts.note: ta is British slang for thank you

indicators.note: something held in an embrace is enclosed, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive adds nothing
the end of the word week is K

explanation.surface: Grateful for a weekend away cuddled by a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weekend' is not Saturday and Sunday but the end of 'week', its last letter K, which goes inside LOVER.
explanation.definitionFit: To reason with someone is to persuade them by discussion, so talk them round.

clue.text: Relaxed note written by high-minded individual in debt

indicators.note: in places the note and saint inside the word for debt

parts.note: to be in debt is to be in the red
E is a musical note
ST is the abbreviation for saint, a virtuous person

explanation.surface: A saint jots a note though deep in debt, yet stays calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'written by' sets the note beside the saint before 'in' places them; 'in the red' is the idiom for owing money.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has rested has taken a break and is refreshed and at ease.

clue.text: A low-growing plant-though it does grow high in Europe

definitions.text: A low-growing plant-though it does grow high in Europe

parts.words: A low-growing plant-though it does grow high in Europe
parts.note: a small alpine flower that keeps low but lives high in the Alps

explanation.definitionFit: Edelweiss is a small white alpine flower found on high Alpine slopes.

clue.text: Misuse of exotic seed container

indicators.note: exotic means strange or foreign, so the letters of seed take an unusual new order

parts.note: a crate is a container

explanation.surface: A foreign seed's packing box is put to wrong use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misuse' is a verb here, not a noun, and 'exotic' is the anagram signal rather than a description of the seed.
explanation.definitionFit: To desecrate a holy place is to treat it with irreverence, abusing it.

clue.text: Tangled line had to be drawn in

indicators.note: a tangled line is twisted up, so its letters and those of had are jumbled

explanation.surface: A knotted fishing line had to be reeled in.
explanation.definitionFit: Air that has been inhaled has been breathed in, pulled into the lungs.

clue.text: The left, being mean, put on airs

parts.note: near is an old word for stingy, mean
side is a British word for pretension, as in putting on side

explanation.surface: A political left that is stingy and also pretentious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The left' is the side of a vehicle nearest the kerb in Britain, where traffic drives on the left.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain the nearside of a car is its left side, by the kerb.

clue.text: A case of very few being in time

indicators.note: being in tells us one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a date is a time
IV is four in Roman numerals, a very small number

explanation.surface: A few cases arrived on time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' is grammatical: in Latin the dative is the case of the indirect object.
explanation.definitionFit: The dative is a grammatical case used for an indirect object.

clue.text: The medium is required to state age

parts.note: to aver is to state firmly

explanation.surface: A clairvoyant must declare how old they are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'medium' looks like a psychic but means the middle value.
explanation.definitionFit: The mean or middle value is the typical, ordinary figure.

clue.text: Money advanced by a rascal to others

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child, a rascal
the rest are the others

explanation.surface: A scamp lends cash to everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: An imprest is a cash advance, such as funds given ahead to an official.

clue.text: Dieting problem that's made light of

indicators.note: a problem leaves things in disorder, so the letters of Dieting are rearranged

explanation.surface: A slimming difficulty that people laughed off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made light of' looks like 'treated as trivial', but here it means set alight.
explanation.definitionFit: Something set alight has been set burning, so made into a source of light.

clue.text: End-of-play announcement

parts.note: a speech delivered to the audience at the close of a drama

explanation.definitionFit: An epilogue is a closing speech addressed to the audience after a play.

clue.text: This enzyme for energy's popular

parts.note: pep is energy, with the possessive giving the S
in means fashionable, popular

explanation.surface: An enzyme for vigour is in fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: Pepsin is a digestive enzyme in the stomach that breaks down proteins.

clue.text: Think twice about the rate increase

parts.note: tempo is a rate of speed
a rise is an increase

explanation.surface: Advice to hesitate before raising interest rates.
explanation.definitionFit: To temporise is to delay or stall, avoiding a decision for now.

clue.text: Support round about a thousand — that's most important

indicators.note: round says the support goes around the other pieces

parts.note: a pier is a pillar that supports
re means about, concerning
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Backing for roughly a grand is what matters most.
explanation.definitionFit: Premier means first in rank, the leading or chief one.

clue.text: Savoury though far from well-cooked morsel

parts.note: rare meat is lightly cooked
a bit is a morsel

explanation.surface: A tasty bite, though it is underdone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Savoury' is a noun: in Britain a savoury is a small salty dish; rarebit is cheese on toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh rarebit, melted cheese on toast, is a classic British savoury dish.

clue.text: Examine some fishes' fins (pectoral fins)

indicators.note: some says only part of the following words is used

explanation.surface: Study a fish's fins, especially its pectorals.
explanation.definitionFit: To inspect is to look over closely, scrutinise.

clue.text: The patrician giving information meant maybe to pocket cash

parts.note: gen is British slang for information

indicators.note: to pocket is to take inside, so one piece goes within the other
maybe suggests the letters of meant could be arranged otherwise

parts.note: L stands for pound, money

explanation.surface: A nobleman giving out details perhaps intended to take money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges MEANT to TEMAN, and 'to pocket' puts L inside it after the T.
explanation.definitionFit: A gentleman, in the old sense, is a man of good birth, an aristocrat.
